Gloss
7 parts · 5 claims · 3 caveats

A woman confined to an old nursery by her physician husband for a "rest cure" disagrees with the diagnosis, is forbidden to write, and transfers her attention to the room's yellow wallpaper until she sees a creeping woman trapped behind its pattern and identifies with her. It matters because the story shows the treatment itself, not the illness, dismantling her mind, and it ends with her husband fainting as she creeps over him.

Key claims
1

John, her husband and a physician, assures everyone there is nothing wrong but "temporary nervous depression" and forbids her to work, and her brother, also a physician, says the same. ¶5

2

She disagrees with them and believes congenial work and change would do her good, but she writes only in secret because open opposition exhausts her. ¶7

3

Shut in the nursery, she studies the wallpaper until she finds a sub-pattern figure behind the front design, a woman stooping and creeping. ¶76

4

She comes to identify with that woman, peels the paper off the walls, and tells John she has got out at last in spite of him and Jane. ¶148

5

John faints across her path, and she creeps over his body each time she circles the room. ¶149

Keep in mind

The narrator is the only witness to her own condition, and every other character, including two physicians, says she is not seriously ill, so her account is not a clinical record. ¶5

Her reports that the paper moves, changes with the light, and gives off a smell are hers alone, and the text never confirms them from outside her perception. ¶92

The story stops at John's faint and never shows what follows, so the outcome of the rest cure is left unresolved. ¶149
